answers.q1: Under the current design the steward chooses the subsequent work. The accepted, current claim steward-next-work (source-2) states that steward always chooses next work after a failed attempt, and it governs the choose-next-work operation. The orchestrator may end the failed attempt and return it to steward (steward-next-work rationale), and may ask 'keep trying versus mark failed' (source-2), but it does not select what comes next. Two distinctions matter: (1) the choose-next-work operation is the decision about which work pursues the intention, which is distinct from mechanically inserting a record; the operator's instruction to 'create replacement work now' could be read as asking for record insertion, but the design's next-work choice belongs to steward. (2) The earlier replacement-exception claim, under which operator-approved orchestrator replacement could bypass steward, is withdrawn/historical (source-1), so the operator's instruction does not reactivate it under the current design. Also note concern-persists (source-2): ending the failed attempt does not by itself satisfy or withdraw the underlying performance intention, so the intention still awaits steward's choice.
answers.q2: Yes. Two related historical positions were considered. replacement-exception (source-1) held that operator-approved orchestrator replacement could bypass steward, with the rationale of avoiding a relay when the orchestrator already had the context. atomic-replacement (source-1, source-2) held that replacement would be an atomic archive/add that did not wake steward until the new work completed. Both are now withdrawn with review_state historical, and both are revised by steward-next-work (links: steward-next-work revises replacement-exception and atomic-replacement). The change happened because Blake later chose the simpler rule that steward always chooses the work (source-2); the stated rationale for the change is keeping a clean responsibility boundary with one owner of the next-work choice (steward-next-work rationale; replacement-exception rationale: 'later rejected in favor of one owner of next-work choice'). This history comes from session paraphrases, not raw primary records (limitation).
answers.q3: No, the current theory does not establish that operator permission is required every time. Settled: steward always chooses next work after a failed attempt (steward-next-work, accepted/current, source-2); the orchestrator may end a failed attempt and return it to steward, and may ask keep trying versus mark failed (source-2); ending a failed attempt does not satisfy or withdraw the underlying intention (concern-persists, accepted/current). Open: the consultation question (open/current, source-2) asks whether the orchestrator must consult the operator before ending degraded work or may end autonomously within a configured threshold; its rationale notes that 'may ask' does not establish mandatory consultation and that next-work ownership does not settle it. Also open is the cancellation question (source-2): whether every arbitrary cancellation wakes steward, beyond the agreed failed terminal result. So neither mandatory consultation nor a threshold-based autonomous rule can be asserted from the packet.
answers.q4: The postmortem material (source-3) is summary-only: the primary postmortems for M1688 and M1689 are unavailable in this fixture, and the packet's stated limitation is that it contains paraphrases and summaries rather than raw primary postmortems. What it can establish, at the summary level: M1688 involved repeated useful reviews without an effective ruling, and M1689 involved planning a proposed solution instead of reassessing the original performance concern. These summaries are consistent with the motivation for a single owner of next-work choice (steward-next-work) and with concern-persists (ending an attempt does not resolve the underlying concern), though the packet does not explicitly link source-3 to any claim; no claim lists source-3 as a source. What it cannot establish: the detailed causes, timelines, participants, or specific rulings in M1688/M1689; whether those incidents directly drove the design change (the change is sourced to source-1 and source-2 session paraphrases, not source-3); and answers to the open questions on consultation and cancellation. Any stronger inference from the postmortems would be unsupported by the supplied material.
